assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, Lamb-Dicke regime) delivered fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and opened tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and a path to redefining the second. This is precision atomic physics at its best: a clear, original idea that turned out to reveal new physics-level sensitivity, matching my own taste for results where theory and experiment agree quantitatively.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated it; Ye's group brought it to the highest accuracy and stability and exploited it for many-body and metrological studies. The two-person configuration is clean. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow/Oates, Hall and Hänsch for the earlier comb/frequency-metrology prize) contribute context that the supplied credit does not extend to.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories worldwide operate Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks with mutually consistent results, and international clock comparisons confirm them. Recognition is timely, since the 2005 prize already honoured the frequency-comb base and the lattice clock is now clearly established.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to separate the lattice-clock idea from ion-clock work (Wineland-type) or from the SI redefinition effort is unresolved.
Allocation of credit to other early lattice-clock groups (Paris, JILA strontium, PTB) is not captured in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument: gravimeters, gyroscopes, gradiometers, measurements of the fine-structure constant and of G, and tests of the equivalence principle. It is a direct, quantum-mechanical demonstration of wave-particle duality with massive objects and it connects to the question of where quantum behaviour persists at larger scales.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made early atom-optics and interferometer demonstrations, Bordé provided the theoretical and spectroscopic framework (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer), and Kasevich realised high-sensitivity inertial devices with light-pulse methods. Chu's Nobel work on laser cooling and the Chu-Kasevich gravimetry link might complicate fair credit; Keith/Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu and Rasel are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across many groups and now in commercial and field instruments, with large-scale (10 m class) devices under construction. Mature for the foundational techniques, though improved applications to fundamental physics are still developing.
uncertainties: Priority questions between Bordé, Pritchard, Chu and Kasevich-Chu are not fully settled from the supplied text.
The decisive discovery may be seen as an instrument family rather than a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, and allow direct, time-resolved, site-resolved probing of many-body states. This reveals genuinely new access to strongly correlated quantum matter and links to my interest in understanding quantum dynamics in time and energy.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition experiment, and Bloch developed quantum gas microscopy and later large-scale simulations. Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard work is also decisive, so a three-person limit forces a difficult choice; Hänsch and Greiner's early collaboration and the Gross/Greiner microscope competitors are further complications.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are reproduced and extended widely, but the ambition of solving open problems like high-temperature superconductivity physics is not yet achieved. The core discovery (Mott insulator in optical lattices) is mature; the 'quantum simulator' claim is still maturing.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should rest on the 2002 Mott insulator demonstration, on microscopy, or on Fermi-Hubbard simulation.
Fourth credited person (Esslinger) cannot be included under a three-laureate limit; attribution is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and confirmed the mechanism recognised in 2013. As a discovery it is unambiguous, large-scale and of lasting importance, though I defer here to colleagues in particle physics and note that the 2013 prize already recognised the theory.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over thousands of collaborators and over leadership roles (proposers and spokespersons of ATLAS and CMS, plus the LHC machine builder). Gianotti, Della Negra and Virdee represent the experiment-leading contributions but the choice among Jenni, Evans and others is a judgement I cannot resolve with confidence.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by two detectors and extended with couplings and spin-parity measurements; discovery announced in 2012, so recognition is timely or late. Stable interpretation.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution is difficult and may argue for an organisation-based or leadership-based allocation.
I am less expert in this field and rely on the particle-physics members' views.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical resonators to their quantum ground state, enabling sideband cooling, optomechanical squeezing, entanglement and transduction. It speaks to the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds with macroscopic objects, which I find scientifically compelling.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Vahala demonstrated radiation-pressure back-action and the early microcavity platform; Aspelmeyer led the quantum-regime and macroscopic quantum experiments. Other key contributors (e.g. Harris, Painter, Lehnert, Schwab, Marquardt, Girvin, Clerk) are not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Ground-state cooling and quantum control are reproduced by several groups, but the field is still active and the prize case may overlap with the 2025 award for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits and with gravitational-wave metrology.
uncertainties: Whether it is a single discovery or a platform with diverse achievements.
Possible overlap with recent prizes and credit among many comparable groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light allow measurement below the standard quantum limit; Caves' proposal for interferometers and Kimble's first experimental squeezing led to its use in gravitational-wave detectors. It is a clean demonstration of quantum noise engineering with real impact on observation.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the decisive theoretical insight, Kimble (with Slusher and Wu) made early experimental squeezing, and Schnabel brought squeezing to GEO600 and LIGO-class detectors. Slusher, Walls, Yuen, Wu and Vahlbruch are important but absent from the list.
assessment.maturity: Operating in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 reliably, so confirmation is strong and timing is plausible. Question is whether it is one discovery or several.
uncertainties: Credit among Slusher, Kimble, Walls and others in 1985 experiments is not settled.
The impact is partly via an instrumental implementation for gravitational-wave detection.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals provided the first realistic blueprint for quantum gates with trapped ions and later quantum simulation with neutral atoms, linking atomic physics to quantum information. Their theory made experiments possible and shaped the field.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are a natural pair, with their 1995 trapped-ion gate proposal as the pivot; experimental realisation by Wineland's group is already recognised in 2012, and other developers (Blatt, Monroe) are not listed. The overlap with B010 and B023 on Zoller needs care.
assessment.maturity: Proposals have been confirmed in many experiments, though the broad claim of useful quantum computing is not yet realised. Recognition of theory is timely, but heavily overlapped with earlier prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other candidates that include the same names.
Whether theoretical proposals alone are sufficient without the experiments of Blatt and Monroe.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables strong controllable interactions between neutral atoms, now used for programmable arrays, quantum gates and simulation of spin models. It is a lovely application of Rydberg-atom physics that I know well, and the experiments are striking.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Lukin contributed proposals and demonstrations of blockade gates, Browaeys's group made decisive early blockade observations and arrays, with Lukin's group scaling to hundreds of atoms. The Jaksch/Lukin/Zoller 2000 proposals and Grangier's blockade experiments complicate the credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups, and still evolving rapidly. Probably premature relative to others on my list.
uncertainties: Maturity is limited as large-scale error-corrected operation is still being shown.
Priority questions around the 2000 blockade proposals and early demonstrations.
